messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Uncertainty: Uncertainty, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kai is a 24-year-old painter who lives with his girlfriend in a small apartment on the outskirts of a midsized city. He came to therapy at her urging, after months of what she described as him "living like a ghost." The event that fractured his life happened eighteen months ago, when he was still living with his previous partner, a man named Derek. What began as verbal jabs during arguments escalated one night into Derek shoving him against a wall, then pinning him to the floor with a knee on his chest while screaming inches from his face. Kai remembers the pressure in his ribs, the spit on his cheek, and then nothing—a complete blank where the next several minutes should be. Other moments from that night, like the sound of a lamp shattering or the sight of his own hand gripping the carpet, are burned into his mind with excruciating clarity, but he cannot arrange them in any order that makes sense. The gaps terrify him more than the images do, because he is certain that what he cannot remember must be the worst part.

In the months that followed, Kai found himself unable to shake the feeling that he was fundamentally the kind of person this happens to. He had always struggled with a quiet sense of inadequacy, but now it crystallized into a fixed belief: the event happened because of who he was, and that meant he no longer belonged anywhere—not in his old life, not in his new relationship, not even in his own body. This conviction colored everything. When his girlfriend would ask him a simple question, he would feel a spike of dread, certain she was about to see through him. He began to notice that any moment of uncertainty—a text left unread, a delay in her response—triggered a cascade of unwanted thoughts about Derek finding him again. The uncertainty itself became a trigger, and soon he was scanning for exits the moment he entered any room, listening for footsteps at the door, and interpreting any delay as evidence that something terrible was unfolding just out of sight. The more he believed he was inadequate and did not belong, the more he watched for threats, and the more he watched, the more triggers he found.

The triggers, in turn, fed back into his memory. A sudden silence in the apartment would drop him straight back into that night, reliving the pressure on his chest as if it were happening right then. The reliving episodes were disorienting and fragmented, and each one deepened his confusion about what had actually happened, which made him feel even more broken and worthless. He started avoiding anything that reminded him of Derek—certain streets, the time of evening when the attack had occurred, even the smell of a particular cologne. He also began to freeze completely when he felt threatened, unable to move or speak, which only reinforced his sense of inadequacy. These strategies, meant to protect him, actually made things worse: avoiding triggers meant he never tested his fears, so the memories stayed raw and unpredictable, and freezing left him feeling humiliated and even more convinced that he was the sort of person who deserved what happened.

The cycle tightened. Every time he froze, the memory of the attack felt more vivid and more out of his control. Every time he scanned for exits, he noticed new potential threats, which triggered more intrusive thoughts, which sent him back into the fragmented reliving. He began to monitor for sounds of someone entering the apartment obsessively, and this hypervigilance made him irritable and exhausted. His girlfriend started to feel like she was walking on eggshells, and Kai, noticing her hesitation, interpreted it as proof that he no longer belonged in this relationship either. The strategies that were supposed to keep him safe were, in his mind, the very things that confirmed he was broken.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at work. He was painting a ceiling in a client's living room when the homeowner, a large man, walked in without warning. Kai dropped his roller, scrambled down the ladder, and stood frozen in the corner, unable to speak or move for nearly a minute. The man was apologetic, confused, and eventually concerned. Kai drove home shaking, and that night he told his girlfriend he could not keep living this way. He is afraid that he will never feel safe again, and that the person he was before the attack is gone for good. But beneath that, in the quietest part of himself, he is most afraid that his worst appraisal is correct—that the event happened because of who he is, and that no amount of therapy can change that.
